# Soil Carbon Recovery Following Tidal Reconnection of Drained Marshland

## Abstract

We measured soil organic carbon in twelve estuarine sites over a six-year period
following the breaching of historic flood dykes. Reconnected sites accumulated
carbon at a mean rate of 1.4 tonnes per hectare per year, significantly higher
than the unmanaged controls. The results suggest that tidal reconnection is an
effective and low-cost method of restoring carbon storage in degraded coastal
landscapes.

## Introduction

Drained coastal marshland releases stored carbon as the exposed peat oxidises.
Reflooding these soils has been proposed as a mitigation measure, but field
evidence on the rate and durability of recovery remains limited. This study
addresses that gap with a multi-site longitudinal dataset.

## Methods

Twelve sites were selected along a single temperate estuary, six reconnected to
the tide and six retained as drained controls. At each site we collected soil
cores to a depth of thirty centimetres at annual intervals. Cores were dried,
weighed, and analysed for organic carbon by loss-on-ignition. Salinity and water
table depth were logged continuously.

## Results

Reconnected sites showed a consistent increase in soil organic carbon across all
six years. By the final survey the mean carbon stock at reconnected sites exceeded
the controls by 22 percent. The accumulation rate was highest in the first two
years and then plateaued as the vegetation matured.

## Discussion

The observed recovery rates are consistent with the upper range reported in
laboratory mesocosm studies. The early plateau suggests that the rapid initial
gain reflects sediment trapping by new vegetation rather than long-term peat
formation, which would imply that durability depends on continued sediment supply.

## Conclusion

Tidal reconnection restores soil carbon storage quickly and at low cost. Long-term
monitoring beyond the six-year window of this study is needed to confirm that the
recovered carbon remains stable.
